729.title: The hidden gift
729.hook: Zhuangzi's hunchback Shu is spared the army and fed by the state (Zhuangzi 4)
729.howItsDone: Readers of the Zhuangzi, Daoists among them, read Shu and the useless tree together as stories about the use of the useless, and some return to them in times of illness, disability or failure.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hukam, the order no one is outside of. Your line was within the order. What did you go with today instead of fighting? Now a new week, and a strange, funny teacher from ancient China. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

The recruiters have come to town. They're rounding up men for the army, and every young man with a strong back has found somewhere to hide: the hayloft, an aunt's house, the reeds by the river. Except one. He's strolling right down the middle of the street, arms swinging, saying hello to the officers. Nobody stops him. Nobody even looks twice. His name, in the book of Zhuangzi, is Shu, and the reason nobody drafts him is his body. Today, a story about what a limit can quietly hold.
screen: `THE RECRUITERS COME TO TOWN.` → `EVERYONE HIDES. EXCEPT ONE.` → `HIS NAME IS SHU.`

segments.voice: First, who Shu is. Zhuangzi describes him in big, almost cartoon strokes: his chin tucked down by his navel, his shoulders higher than the top of his head, his hair knot pointing at the sky. It's a body that fits none of the world's measures. Second, how he lives. He isn't helpless in the story. He earns his food sewing and washing clothes, and by sifting grain he makes enough to feed others besides himself. Third, the turn. When the army comes, he walks among the recruiters without fear. When the state calls up men for heavy labor, he's excused, because of his condition. And when the state hands out grain to the sick, he gets his share, and firewood too. Then Zhuangzi draws the lesson, in paraphrase: if a man whose body is out of the usual shape can look after himself and live out his years, how much more someone whose virtue is out of the usual shape. This whole chapter is set in a dangerous world, where being useful gets you used up. This path met the useless tree in its first year; Shu is its neighbor in the same chapter. And the chapter ends, in paraphrase: everyone knows the use of the useful, but nobody knows the use of the useless. Fourth, what it isn't. Zhuangzi doesn't say every limit is secretly a blessing, and nobody gets to tell you yours is. He turns the picture, once, to show a side the world's measuring stick misses. The gift is hidden, partial, and still real.
screen: `A BODY THAT FITS NO MEASURE.` · `HE EARNS HIS KEEP.` · `SPARED THE ARMY, FED BY THE STATE.` · `NOT A PROMISE. A TURNED PICTURE.` · then, large: `THE USE OF THE USELESS.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one limit you live with. Keep it small enough to hold today: a knee that won't run, a shyness, no car, not enough money for the thing everyone else is doing. Hold it without arguing with it. Then ask it two quiet questions. What do you spare me from? And what do you leave room for? Maybe something comes: a slower walk where you notice more, an evening you didn't have to be anywhere. Maybe nothing comes, and that's an honest answer too. The bell holds the time.
The hidden gift. Zhuangzi's Shu, spared and fed because he didn't fit the world's measure. Not every limit, and not a promise. Just a side the measuring stick misses. Today's word.
Your line: the hidden gift. Today, when a limit gets in your way, ask it once what it spares you, and let the answer be small, or nothing at all. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

730.title: All shall be well
730.hook: Julian is told that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well (Revelations of Divine Love 27)
730.howItsDone: Christians of several churches read Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love, and her line all shall be well is sometimes said or sung in prayer services and at times of grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shu, spared because his body fit none of the world's measures. Your line was the hidden gift. Did a limit spare you anything, or nothing? Today, a sick woman's question, and the answer she heard. Day seven hundred thirty.

All shall be well. Said fast, it can sound like it'll be fine, the kind of thing said over a shoulder on the way out of a room, when nobody knows what else to say. But the woman who wrote it down didn't hear it in passing. She heard it in her sickbed. Julian of Norwich, whom this path met with a hazelnut in her palm, writes that she was so ill the people around her thought she was dying. And she wasn't asking for comfort. She was asking a hard question. Today: what she asked, and what she heard back.
screen: `SAID FAST, IT SOUNDS LIKE: IT'LL BE FINE.` → `JULIAN HEARD IT IN THE BED.` → `SHE WAS ASKING A HARD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the question. In chapter twenty-seven of her Revelations of Divine Love, Julian says she wondered why God, in all his foreseeing wisdom, didn't stop sin at the very beginning. Because then, she thought, all would have been well. It's the old why, asked straight, by someone in pain. Second, the answer. She doesn't get a reason. She hears that sin was behovely, an old word for fitting, something that had its place. And then the line, in Grace Warrack's edition: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Third, the tone. Julian notices how it was said. In her telling, the words came very tenderly, with no blame laid on her, nor on any who shall be saved. Not a lecture. Not a correction for asking. Just a promise, said kindly to a person who had dared the question. Fourth, the tense. Listen to it again: shall. Not all is well. All shall be. Julian doesn't pretend the world in front of her is fine. And she doesn't stop asking either. In the chapters that follow she keeps pressing how it could ever be made well, with so much harm in the world. Later she is told, in paraphrase, that she'll see it herself: that all manner of thing shall be well. So the line isn't an answer that ends the question. It's a promise that keeps her company while the question stays open. Some Christians who read Julian hold it that way, and some readers take it simply as a line from a woman who asked honestly, and was answered gently.
screen: `WHY WASN'T SIN STOPPED AT THE START?` · `NO REASON. A PROMISE.` · `SAID TENDERLY, WITH NO BLAME.` · `SHALL, NOT IS.` · then, large: `ALL SHALL BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow on its own. Bring to mind one thing that is not well right now. In your life, or someone else's. Let it be what it is; you don't need to fix it or explain it. Then, once, silently and slowly, say Julian's line: all shall be well. Only once. Don't repeat it to drown the hard thing out. Notice how it lands. If it rings true, let it. If it rings false today, let that be honest too. If you pray, you can offer it as Julian heard it, as a promise. If you don't, hold it as a line from a book. The bell holds the time.
All shall be well. Julian's words, heard in sickness, in answer to the question why. Not all is well. All shall be. Today's word.
Your line: all shall be well. Today, when something isn't well, say it once, slowly, without forcing it, and then turn back to what's in front of you. Day seven hundred thirty.

731.title: Ivan's rebellion
731.hook: in Dostoevsky, Ivan refuses a harmony bought with a child's tears (The Brothers Karamazov, book 5)
731.howItsDone: Readers, believers and unbelievers alike, return to Ivan's chapter when they think about the problem of suffering, and it's read in literature, philosophy and theology classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Julian, sick in bed, asking why, and hearing a tender promise. Your line was all shall be well. Did you say it once, without forcing it? Today, someone who refuses that kind of promise, for a reason worth hearing. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

A small-town tavern, and two brothers at a table. The younger one, Alyosha, is a novice at the local monastery, gentle, a listener. The older one, Ivan, is brilliant and restless, and tonight he's decided to say out loud what he really thinks. He's been collecting things, he tells his brother. Clippings. Stories. And he isn't going to argue about whether God exists. He's going to argue about something harder. This is Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, and the chapter is called Rebellion. Today: Ivan's rebellion.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS IN A TAVERN.` → `IVAN HAS BEEN COLLECTING THINGS.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED REBELLION.`

segments.voice: First, the collection. Ivan has been gathering true stories, he says, of cruelty done to children. He tells several. They're too hard to repeat here, and that's his point. The grown-ups, he says, have eaten the apple, so to speak; let them answer for it. But the children haven't. Why should they suffer? Second, the refusal. Ivan imagines the end of everything: every wrong explained, everyone embracing, a harmony where all is made right. And he says he doesn't want it, if it costs one child's tears. It isn't worth that price. He's careful about how he says it: it isn't God he refuses, he says. He just, most respectfully, returns his ticket. And Alyosha, quietly, names it: that's rebellion. Third, the question. Ivan turns it on his brother. Suppose you were building the world, to make people happy in the end, at last, and it could only be done by torturing one small child. Would you agree to be the builder on those terms? Tell the truth. And Alyosha, the novice, answers softly: no, I wouldn't consent. Fourth, what the book does next. Alyosha doesn't win the argument. He speaks of one who can forgive everything, because he gave his own innocent blood. Ivan answers with a long poem about a Grand Inquisitor. And when the poem ends, Alyosha doesn't rebut it. He leans over and kisses his brother. Dostoevsky lets the question stand at full strength, in the mouth of a character he gave strong arguments to. This whole block has listened to Job, the cross, the Quran's patience, Julian's promise. Ivan is the voice that says: not at that price. The novel gives him his full say, and so does this day.
screen: `STORIES OF CHILDREN WHO SUFFERED.` · `I RETURN MY TICKET.` · `WOULD YOU BUILD IT ON ONE CHILD?` · `A KISS, NOT A REBUTTAL.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION STAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow a little. Bring to mind one hard question you can't answer. Why that happened to them. Why it goes on. Don't pick the heaviest one you own; pick one you can hold for two minutes. Now hold it like a stone in your open hand. The mind will reach for an answer, or reach for the exit. Each time it does, notice, and set the question gently back in your palm. You're not solving it. You're letting it be a real question, the way Ivan and Alyosha did at that table. The bell holds the time.
Ivan's rebellion. In The Brothers Karamazov, his refusal of any harmony bought with a child's tears. A question the novel lets stand. Today's word.
Your line: the question stays. Today, if a hard why comes up, yours or someone else's, don't rush to close it. Let it stay open a little longer. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

732.title: Meaning, even here
732.hook: Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who was held in the Nazi camps, argued meaning can be found even in suffering (Man's Search for Meaning)
732.howItsDone: Frankl's approach, which he called logotherapy, is taught in some counseling and psychotherapy training, and his book is read by people facing grief, illness and loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ivan at the tavern table, returning his ticket, and Alyosha answering with a kiss. Your line was the question stays. Did you let a hard why stay open? Today, a doctor who asked a different question. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

An older doctor comes to see a psychiatrist. His wife has died, and he can't get out from under the grief. He loved her above everything, he says. The psychiatrist doesn't offer advice. He asks a question instead: what would have happened if you had died first, and she had been left to go on without you? The man answers: for her, that would have been terrible. How she would have suffered. The psychiatrist was Viktor Frankl, and he tells this story in Man's Search for Meaning. Today: what happened next, and the word underneath it.
screen: `AN OLDER DOCTOR, GRIEVING.` → `WHAT IF YOU HAD DIED FIRST?` → `HOW SHE WOULD HAVE SUFFERED.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Frankl answers the doctor, in paraphrase: you see, she was spared that suffering, and it was you who spared her, at the price of surviving her and mourning her. The man says nothing more. He shakes Frankl's hand and leaves. Nothing about the loss has changed. The grief is still there. But, Frankl writes, it now had a meaning: a sacrifice made for her. Second, where Frankl learned this. Before he wrote that, he had been a prisoner in the Nazi camps, Auschwitz among them, and the first part of his book is his plain account of that time. He doesn't write it as a hero story. He writes about hunger, cold, and what he saw people do, the worst and the best. Third, the claim. Frankl names ways a person finds meaning: by doing a deed or making something, by loving someone or experiencing something, and, when suffering can't be avoided, by the stance a person takes toward it. That third way is today's. Fourth, what he doesn't say. Frankl is careful here. Suffering isn't needed for meaning, he says. If suffering can be avoided, the meaningful thing is to remove it, whether it's the cause or the pain. Choosing pain you don't have to bear isn't heroic, in his words; it's just needless. Meaning is not the reason something hard happens. It's something a person can still find, or make, inside it. And no one gets to hand it to someone else. The doctor found his own, in answer to a question.
screen: `YOU SPARED HER THAT.` · `A PRISONER IN THE CAMPS.` · `DEED, LOVE, AND THE STANCE YOU TAKE.` · `IF YOU CAN END IT, END IT.` · then, large: `MEANING, EVEN HERE.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle, and let the breath go at its own pace. Bring to mind one hard thing in your life now. A caregiving season, a job you can't leave yet, a loss. Not the hardest thing; one you can hold. Then ask it Frankl's kind of question, gently. Who is this for? What am I carrying, and for whom? What could this make possible, even something small? If an answer comes, let it be modest. If none comes, that's allowed: the question can wait. You're not grading the hard thing. Just looking for one thread of meaning in it. The bell holds the time.
Meaning. For Frankl, what a person can still find in deeds, in love, and, when suffering can't be avoided, in how they bear it. Not the reason for the pain. Today's word.
Your line: meaning, even here. Today, inside one hard or boring task, ask once who it's for. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

733.title: The last freedom
733.hook: Frankl: the freedom to choose one's attitude can't be taken (Man's Search for Meaning)
733.howItsDone: Readers of Frankl, and some counselors trained in his logotherapy, practice noticing the space between what happens and how they respond, and choosing a stance toward what they can't change.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Frankl and the grieving doctor, and a question that gave a loss its meaning. Your line was meaning, even here. Who was your hard task for? Today, a piece of bread in the evening. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

Evening, in a prisoners' hut. Everyone is starving. The daily ration is a little bread and thin soup, and every crumb counts. And Frankl remembers men who walked through the huts comforting others, and giving away their last piece of bread. He says there may have been few of them. But they were there. And for him, that was proof of something. Not about how strong they were. About what can and can't be taken from a person. Today: the last freedom.
screen: `EVENING IN A PRISONERS' HUT.` → `MEN WHO GAVE AWAY THEIR LAST BREAD.` → `WHAT CAN'T BE TAKEN?`

segments.voice: First, what was taken. Frankl's account of the camps is a list of losses: his name replaced by a number, his clothes, his hair, his manuscript, and no knowledge of whether the people he loved were alive. Everything a person usually leans on, gone. Second, what wasn't. Out of watching those men in the huts, Frankl draws his conclusion, in paraphrase: everything can be taken from a person but one thing, the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given circumstances, to choose one's own way. Third, how small it can be. In his account, this freedom isn't a grand speech. It's a shared crust. A kind word to the man in the next bunk. Once, marching in the cold, Frankl kept himself going by picturing himself in a warm lecture hall, describing the camp as something to be studied. That was his own way: turning toward the suffering as something to understand, not only something to endure. Fourth, what it isn't. This is not a grade for anyone in pain. Frankl writes as a witness, not a judge, and the freedom he describes is a door that's there, not a test some people fail. And it doesn't excuse anyone who causes suffering. The camps were a crime; the freedom he found inside them doesn't make them less of one. It just means that even there, one small choice was still a person's own: the stance they took toward what was happening.
screen: `WHAT WAS TAKEN: ALMOST EVERYTHING.` · `WHAT WASN'T: HOW TO MEET IT.` · `A CRUST. A KIND WORD. A LECTURE HALL.` · `A DOOR, NOT A GRADE.` · then, large: `THE LAST FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one small thing from today that happened without asking you: a changed schedule, a person's mood, a late bus, an ache. Let it be there. Then notice there's still a small space between it and you: the space where you decide how to meet it. You don't have to fill that space with anything big. Try a few words for it: patient, curious, kind, honest, steady. See which one fits today. Let it settle into the body. The bell holds the time.
The last freedom. Frankl's phrase for what couldn't be taken, even in the camps: choosing how to meet what's happening. Today's word.
Your line: my attitude. Today, when something happens that you didn't choose, take one breath and pick the word you'll meet it with. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

734.title: Water at the pump
734.hook: water on one hand, the word spelled into the other, and Helen Keller's locked world opens (The Story of My Life, 4)
734.howItsDone: Readers come back to Helen Keller's account of the well house when they think about language, teaching and breakthrough, and the scene is retold in schools and on stage.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last freedom, and the men who gave away their bread. Your line was my attitude. Which word did you meet the day with? Today, a well house, and one word that opened a world. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

A broken doll lies on the floor by the hearth. The girl who smashed it feels nothing about it, she later writes: no sorrow, no regret. She can't see and she can't hear, and her teacher has been spelling words into her hand day after day, letters pressed into the palm with quick fingers. The girl can copy the shapes. She has no idea they mean anything. So her teacher takes her by the hand, out into the warm day, down the path to the well house, where someone is drawing water at the pump. Today: water at the pump.
screen: `A BROKEN DOLL BY THE HEARTH.` → `LETTERS PRESSED INTO A PALM.` → `DOWN THE PATH TO THE PUMP.`

segments.voice: First, the two hands. This is Helen Keller's own account, in chapter four of The Story of My Life. Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, puts one of Helen's hands under the spout. Cool water rushes over it. Into the other hand she spells w-a-t-e-r, slowly at first, then fast. Helen stands still, all her attention on those moving fingers. Second, the opening. Something like a forgotten memory stirs, she writes, and the mystery of language comes open. In her words: "I knew then that 'w-a-t-e-r' meant the wonderful cool something that was flowing over my hand." Not a shape in the palm. A name for a thing. And if this had a name, everything did. Third, the doll. On the way back to the house, she writes, every object she touched seemed to be alive. She remembers the doll she broke. She feels her way to the hearth, picks up the pieces, and tries, uselessly, to put them together. And now, she says, her eyes filled with tears. She understood what she had done, and she was sorry. A word for water, and then a word for wrong. Fourth, why it's here, in a block on suffering. Her account doesn't say the dark and the silence went away. They didn't. What changed was that she was no longer alone inside them. Someone had reached in with a name, and a word became a bridge between two people. In her book she calls it a living word, one that set her soul free. Not a cure. A way through.
screen: `WATER ON ONE HAND, A WORD IN THE OTHER.` · `THE MYSTERY OF LANGUAGE OPENS.` · `BACK TO THE BROKEN DOLL.` · `NOT A CURE. A WAY THROUGH.` · then, large: `WATER.`

segments.voice: If you have water near you, a glass, a sink, a bottle, let it touch your hand: a few drops on the palm, or your fingers around the cold glass. If you don't, remember the last time water ran over your hands. Close your eyes if you like. Feel only that: cool, wet, moving or still. Then, slowly, trace the letters of the word with a finger of the other hand on your palm: w, a, t, e, r. Feel the thing and its name meet. Let the rest of the room go quiet around it. The bell holds the time.
Water at the pump. Helen Keller's moment at the well house, when a word spelled into her hand met the water on the other, and her locked world opened. Today's word.
Your line: water. Today, the next time water touches your hands, at a sink or in the rain, stop for one breath, feel it, and name it. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

735.title: No ranking
735.hook: the voices of this block keep company with pain; none of them asks anyone to rank it or compare it to someone else's
735.howItsDone: In Jewish mourning, visitors to a shiva house may wait for the mourner to speak first, and Christians read Romans 12:15 as a call to share both joy and grief; some chaplains and counselors are taught not to compare one person's pain with another's.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Helen Keller at the pump, water on one hand and the word in the other. Your line was water. Did you stop and name it? Today, the end of a week, and a habit worth dropping. Day seven hundred thirty-five.

"At least it's not cancer." "Other people have it so much worse." "I shouldn't complain, after what she's been through." These lines get said with the best intentions, sometimes to a friend, often to ourselves. They sound humble. But listen to what they do. They put pain on a scale, and somebody's pain has to lose. Across this whole block, from Job to Julian to Frankl, the texts keep company with suffering in many ways. They don't line it up and rank it. Today: no ranking.
screen: `AT LEAST IT'S NOT...` → `PAIN ON A SCALE.` → `SOMEBODY ALWAYS LOSES.`

segments.voice: First, Job's friends, at their best. When they arrive and see him, the King James Bible says: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." They didn't measure it against anyone's. They sat in it with him. It's when they start talking, explaining and weighing, that the book turns against them. Second, Paul's line to the church in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Weep with. Not weigh against. Paul sets it in a list of ways to live alongside each other. Third, Frankl, a man who had every reason to rank. In Man's Search for Meaning he offers a picture, in paraphrase: suffering behaves like a gas in an empty room. A little gas or a lot, it fills the whole room. So a person's suffering, great or small, fills the whole of them. The size of suffering, he says, is relative, and comparing doesn't shrink anything. Fourth, the week. Shu showed a gift the world's measure missed. Julian heard a promise said with no blame. Ivan refused to let one child's tears be outweighed. Frankl found meaning inside the camps, and Helen found a word at the pump. Not one of them asked anyone to prove their pain was big enough to count. Ranking doesn't make anyone's pain smaller. It just leaves someone alone with theirs.
screen: `JOB'S FRIENDS SAT, AND SAID NOTHING.` · `WEEP WITH, NOT WEIGH AGAINST.` · `LIKE A GAS, IT FILLS THE ROOM.` · `A WEEK WITH NO SCALE.` · then, large: `NO RANKING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind something that hurts in your life right now, big or small. Notice if a voice shows up to compare it: at least, others have it worse, I shouldn't. When it does, set the scale down. You don't have to argue with the voice. Just let your own thing be the size it is. Then, if you like, bring to mind someone else who's hurting, and let theirs be the size it is too. Two pains, side by side, neither one weighed. The bell holds the time.
No ranking. Pain kept company with, not weighed against anyone else's: weep with them that weep. Today's word.

Your line: no ranking. This week: the hidden gift, all shall be well, the question stays, meaning, the last freedom, water, and no ranking. Today, catch one at least, in your mouth or your head, and let it go unsaid. Day seven hundred thirty-five.

myth: Job's friends went wrong the moment they arrived
at first they sat with him in silence; it went wrong when they started explaining.
Frankl compared suffering to a gas that fills a whole room
great or small, it fills the person completely.
Paul's line says to weigh another's grief against your own
it says weep with them that weep.

fork.setup: your friend tells you about a hard week. your own week was much worse. what do you say?
options: at least you didn't have my week.
that sounds hard. tell me about it.
fork.reveal: Job's friends did best when they just sat with him, and Paul's line is weep with, not weigh against. their week fills them the way yours fills you.

trapdoor: what you thought: comparing keeps things in proportion.
what it means: pain fills a person whatever its size; ranking it leaves someone alone with theirs.
what a scholar hears: Job 2:13, where the friends' silence comes before their speeches, and Frankl's gas image in part one of Man's Search for Meaning.

sources.ref: Man's Search for Meaning, part one (suffering like a gas)
